text: This video shows time as an effect, in one strategy.
doeff runs Python functions that yield effects to handlers.
First we read sma_cross, then we put clocks around it.
This is sma_cross, a small trading strategy.
It reads one bar at a time and trades on two averages.
It starts with no closes, no position and no cash.
It yields Tick to get the next bar, until it gets None.
It keeps the close, and skips until it has slow of them.
Then it averages the last fast and the last slow closes.
Fast above slow: it yields Order to buy, then Log.
Fast below slow: it yields Order to sell, then Log.
When Tick gives None, it sells what it still holds.
It returns the cash: the profit of the session.
Tick, Order and Log are values, not calls.
The handlers around it give them their meaning.
recorded answers Tick from 300 saved bars.
paper fills each Order at the last close.
The backtest prints its trades at once: pnl 50.79.
A market sends one bar a minute.
bar_clock first yields Delay(60) for each Tick.
Then it passes that Tick on, and resumes its k with the bar.
virtual_clock answers GetTime with the time it keeps.
For Delay, it parks the task until its wake-up time.
When every task waits, it jumps to that time.
stamped asks GetTime and writes 09:21 on the first trade.
Five hours of bars end at 14:01, in under a second.
wall_clock answers GetTime with the machine's time.
For Delay, it awaits asyncio.sleep, then resumes its k.
await_handler runs that sleep on an asyncio loop.
Sixty bars, 10 ms apart, now take over 0.6 seconds.
Both clocks give the same pnl, 6.85.
sma_cross never changed. Only the clock around it did.
